title: How to Balance Saving for College vs. Saving for Retirement
description: Prioritizing your future over your children's education without guilt.
content:
The most common emotional conflict for parents is the choice between funding their 401(k) and funding a 529 College Plan. You want to give your children a debt-free start, but you also don't want to be a burden on them in your old age. The golden rule of financial planning is: **'You can get a loan for college, but you cannot get a loan for retirement.'** This guide explains why securing your own future is actually the best gift you can give your children, and how to help them with school without sacrificing your nest egg.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Oxygen Mask' Principle: If you arrive at age 65 with $0 savings because you paid for college, your children will have to support you financially. That is a far heavier burden than student loans.
  • The '1/3rd' Funding Goal: Don't aim to pay 100% of college. Aim to pay 1/3 from savings, 1/3 from current income (while they are in school), and 1/3 from student loans. This makes the savings target achievable.
  • Roth IRA as a Dual Tool: Roth IRAs can be used for retirement OR education (penalty-free withdrawals). Prioritize the Roth over the 529 because it offers optionality.
  • The 'State School' Cap: Tell your kids early: "We have saved enough for [State U]. If you want to go to [Private U], you must fund the difference." Manage expectations.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The FAFSA formula assesses student assets (UTMA) heavily (20%) but ignores parental retirement assets (401k/Roth). Saving in a retirement account actually helps your child qualify for more financial aid than saving in a brokerage account.

The Math of Mis-Prioritization

Scenario: You have $500/month surplus.

Option A: All for College (529)

You save $500/mo for 18 years. Result: $175,000 in 529.
Outcome: Kid graduates debt-free. You have $0 for retirement. You work until 75.

Option B: All for Retirement (401k)

You save $500/mo for 18 years. Result: $175,000 in 401k.
Outcome: Kid takes $40,000 in loans. You have a nest egg that compounds for another 15 years to $500,000 by the time you retire.

The Verdict: Option B is safer. The kid can pay off $40k loans with a entry-level salary. You cannot generate $500k of retirement wealth overnight.

Tactical Compromise

  1. Max the Match First: Never put a dollar in a 529 until you have captured 100% of your employer's 401(k) match. That is free money.
  2. Roth IRA Second: Max the Roth. If your kid needs tuition, you can pull the principal. If they get a scholarship, you keep it for retirement. It is the perfect hedge.
  3. 529 Third: Only fund the 529 after you are saving 15% for retirement. Use the 'Superfunding' rule if you get a windfall (inheritance) to catch up.
  4. The 'Secure Act' Safety Valve: New rules allow you to roll unused 529 money ($35k) into a Roth IRA for the child. This removes the fear of 'over-saving' for college.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it selfish to not pay for college?

No. It is responsible. An insolvent parent is a liability. A financially secure parent is an asset. Secure your own ship.

Does 529 hurt financial aid?

Slightly (5.64% assessment). But income hurts aid far more. Don't avoid saving just to game the FAFSA; having cash is always better than hoping for aid.

What about Parent PLUS loans?

Avoid. These are loans you take out. They destroy your retirement cash flow. Let the student take federal loans in their name (capped limits).
